name: Rose
growing: At least 6 hours of sun with good airflow.
Rich, well-drained soil with compost and manure.
Deep weekly soak at the base; avoid wetting leaves.
Rose food in late winter, after each flush and in late summer.
Cut off spent blooms down to the first five-leaflet leaf for repeat flowering.
Main prune in late July–August: remove dead and crossing stems and cut back by about a third to outward buds.
Black spot, powdery mildew, aphids, two-spotted mite.
Buy budded plants; cuttings in autumn.
uses: Hedges, climbers on arches, cut flowers.
Petals for potpourri; hips for tea.

tasks.title: Rose: winter prune
tasks.notes: Cut back by a third to outward buds.

tasks.title: Rose: feed
tasks.notes: Rose food around the drip line.

cautions.text: Non-toxic, but thorns can injure.
Thorns; wear gloves.

summary: Deciduous flowering shrub that blooms from spring to late autumn. Hybrid teas, floribundas, climbers and shrub roses.
harvest: Cut blooms for vases early in the morning.
reminders: Prune late Jul–Aug · feed after each flush · deadhead weekly.

name: Hydrangea
growing: Morning sun with afternoon shade; wilts in hot afternoon sun.
Generous in summer; it wilts quickly when dry.
General feed in spring. Add sulphur for blue flowers, lime for pink.
Late winter: cut stems that flowered back to a pair of fat buds. Leave stems that didn't flower.

tasks.title: Hydrangea: prune
tasks.notes: Cut flowered stems to a pair of fat buds.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats if leaves or flowers are eaten.
Not edible; can cause stomach upset.

summary: Deciduous shrub, 1–2 m, with big summer flower heads. Blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline.
harvest: Cut flowers for vases; old heads dry well.
reminders: Prune late winter · water well in summer.

name: Gardenia
growing: Azalea and camellia fertiliser in spring and late summer.
Yellow leaves often mean cold soil or lack of magnesium; feed with Epsom salts in spring.
uses: Hedges and pots near paths for scent.

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten.

summary: Evergreen shrub with glossy leaves and very fragrant white flowers in late spring and summer.
harvest: Cut flowers to float in a bowl.
reminders: Feed spring and late summer · trim after flowering.

name: Camellia
growing: Part shade; sasanquas take more sun.
Regular, especially when buds are forming in late summer.
Azalea and camellia fertiliser after flowering.
summary: Long-lived evergreen shrubs that flower in autumn (sasanqua) and winter (japonica) in shade.
harvest: Cut stems for vases.
reminders: Feed and prune after flowering · water in late summer.

name: Azalea
growing: Keep moist; shallow roots dry quickly.
Azalea and camellia fertiliser after flowering.
uses: Keep pets and children from eating any part.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs, cats and other animals; even small amounts can cause serious illness.
All parts are toxic if eaten.

summary: Evergreen shrub smothered in flowers in late winter and spring. Shallow-rooted.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Feed and trim after flowering · keep moist.

name: Pelargonium
growing: Full sun; handles heat and coastal conditions.
Liquid feed monthly in the growing season.
Cut back by a third in late summer to stop legginess.

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs and irritate skin.
Some people get skin rashes from the leaves.

summary: Tough perennial flowering most of the year. Zonal, ivy-leaved and scented-leaf types.
harvest: Scented-leaf types can be picked for tea and baking.
reminders: Deadhead · cut back in late summer.

name: Marigold
growing: Snails on seedlings, spider mites in heat.
Seed or seedlings September to January.
uses: Plant among vegetables to attract hoverflies and deter some nematodes.

cautions.text: Can mildly upset pets' stomachs and skin.
Sap can irritate sensitive skin.

summary: Bright annual, 20–60 cm, flowering through the warm months. Classic companion plant.
harvest: Not harvested; seed heads can be saved.
reminders: Plant spring · deadhead.

name: Sunflower
growing: Birds on seeds, snails on seedlings.
Sow seed direct September to January.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Fast annual, 0.5–3 m, with big flowers in summer. Dwarf types suit pots.
harvest: Cut flowers for vases; dry heads for seeds when backs turn brown.
reminders: Sow Sep–Jan · stake tall types.

name: Sweet Pea
growing: Pick flowers often to keep them coming.
Sow seed direct March to May.
uses: Keep seeds away from children and pets.

cautions.text: Seeds and pods are toxic to pets.
Seeds and pods are toxic; not edible like garden peas.

summary: Fragrant climbing annual for cut flowers in late winter and spring. Traditionally sown on St Patrick's Day.
harvest: Pick stems every few days.
reminders: Sow mid-March · trellis · pick often.

name: Nasturtium
growing: Poor soil gives more flowers; rich soil gives leaves.
Aphids and cabbage white caterpillars (useful as a trap crop).
Sow seed direct most of the year.
uses: Salads, pesto; seeds can be pickled like capers.
Trap crop that lures aphids away from vegetables.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Easy sprawling annual with edible peppery leaves and flowers. Self-seeds freely.
harvest: Pick leaves and flowers any time.
reminders: Sow any time · pull extras when they spread.

name: Salvia
growing: Cut back hard in late winter; trim after each flush.

cautions.text: Ornamental salvias are generally considered non-toxic.

summary: Long-flowering perennials, 0.5–2 m, in blue, purple, red and pink. Loved by bees and nectar birds.
harvest: Cut flowers for vases.
reminders: Cut back hard in late winter · trim between flushes.

name: Agapanthus
growing: Cut off spent flower stems before they seed. Some areas list agapanthus as an environmental weed.

cautions.text: Can cause mouth irritation and stomach upset if chewed.
Sap can irritate skin and mouth.

summary: Tough clumping perennial with blue or white flower heads in summer. Handles drought and neglect.
harvest: Cut flowers for vases.
reminders: Remove spent flowers before seeding.

name: Frangipani
growing: Very well-drained; rots in wet soil.
Rarely needed; cut in late winter if required.
Deciduous; bare branches all winter are normal.
Cuttings: let the cut end dry for 2 weeks before potting.

cautions.text: Milky sap can irritate mouths and stomachs.
Sap irritates skin and eyes.

summary: Deciduous small tree, 3–5 m, with fragrant summer flowers. Loves heat; needs a warm, frost-free spot.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Feed in spring · keep dry in winter.

name: Bougainvillea
growing: Well-drained; poor soil gives more flowers.
Low; too much water gives leaves, not colour.
Prune after each flush; hard prune in late winter.
Strong frame or fence for climbing types.

cautions.text: Thorns can injure; sap can mildly irritate.
Sharp thorns; wear gloves.

summary: Vigorous thorny climber or shrub with vivid bracts through the warm months. Loves heat and dry soil.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Hard prune late winter · trim after flowering.

name: Lemon
growing: Full sun, sheltered from strong wind.
Well-drained soil with compost; citrus hate wet feet. Mound up in heavy soil.
Deep, regular watering, especially while fruit is forming. Mulch, keeping it off the trunk.
Citrus fertiliser in late winter and late summer; water in well.
Light prune after harvest to open the centre; remove suckers below the graft.
Gall wasp (cut out swollen twigs before September), citrus leaf miner, scale, aphids, bronze orange bug.
Yellow leaves in winter usually mean cold soil or hunger; feed in spring.
Hardy to light frost once established.
uses: Juice, zest, preserved lemons, dressings, baking.

tasks.title: Lemon: citrus feed
tasks.notes: Citrus fertiliser around the drip line; water in.

tasks.title: Lemon: cut out gall wasp galls

cautions.text: Leaves, peel and oils can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs.
Thorny branches on some varieties. Peel oil can cause skin sensitivity in strong sun.

summary: Evergreen citrus tree, 3–4 m (dwarf types 1.5–2 m), that fruits most of the year. Meyer is sweeter and compact.
harvest: Pick when fully coloured and slightly soft; fruit holds on the tree for weeks.
reminders: Feed late winter and late summer · prune galls before spring · water deeply.

name: Lime
growing: Citrus fertiliser late winter and late summer.
Leaf miner, scale, gall wasp, bronze orange bug.
uses: Drinks, Thai and Mexican dishes, desserts.

cautions.text: Leaves, peel and oils can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs.
Lime juice on skin in sunlight can cause blistering burns (phytophotodermatitis); wash hands.

summary: Compact citrus, 2–3 m, with juicy seedless fruit. Slightly more frost tender than lemon.
harvest: Pick green and glossy, or leave to turn yellow and juicier, mainly late summer to winter.
reminders: Feed late winter and late summer.

name: Orange
growing: Citrus fertiliser late winter and late summer.
Light prune after harvest; remove water shoots.
Gall wasp, leaf miner, scale, bronze orange bug, fruit fly.

cautions.text: Leaves, peel and oils can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs.

summary: Citrus tree, 4–6 m (dwarf 2 m). Navels ripen in winter; Valencias in spring and summer.
harvest: Taste-test; oranges don't ripen further once picked.
reminders: Feed late winter and late summer · prune galls in winter.

name: Mandarin
growing: Citrus fertiliser late winter and late summer.
Thin heavy crops when fruit is marble-sized to reduce biennial bearing.
Fruit fly, gall wasp, leaf miner, scale.

cautions.text: Leaves, peel and oils can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs.

summary: Small citrus tree, 2–4 m, with easy-peel fruit in autumn and winter. Tends to crop heavily every second year.
harvest: Pick when coloured and sweet; don't leave too long or fruit dries out.
reminders: Feed late winter and late summer · thin heavy crops.

name: Strawberry
growing: Full sun with morning shade in hot areas.
Rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; raised beds or pots stop fruit rotting.
Potash-rich liquid feed every 2 weeks while fruiting.
Straw or pine needles under plants keep fruit clean.
Remove runners for bigger fruit, or pot them up for new plants.
Birds, slugs, snails, grey mould in wet weather. Net once fruit forms.
Plant runners or crowns in autumn and winter.
summary: Low perennial that fruits from spring to autumn. Plants are most productive for 2–3 years.
harvest: Pick when fully red, every couple of days.
reminders: Plant in autumn · feed fortnightly while fruiting · net against birds.

name: Blueberry
growing: Full sun; afternoon shade in hot areas.
Acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) and well-drained. Use azalea and camellia mix in pots.
Keep moist; shallow roots dry out fast. Use rainwater if your tap water is hard.
Azalea and camellia fertiliser in spring and summer.
In winter, remove old, unproductive canes.
Plant two varieties for better crops.
uses: Autumn leaf colour on deciduous types.
summary: Deciduous or evergreen shrub, 1–2 m, needing acidic soil. Southern highbush and rabbiteye types suit the coast.
harvest: Pick when fully blue, usually November to February.
reminders: Feed in spring · net fruit · prune old canes in winter.

name: Raspberry
growing: Full sun with shelter from hot wind.
Two-wire trellis to keep canes upright.
Suckers freely; keep to a bed.
Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest; autumn types can be cut to the ground in winter.

cautions.text: Prickly canes; wear gloves.

summary: Cane fruit grown on a trellis. Low-chill and autumn-fruiting types suit the coast best.
harvest: Pick when berries slip easily off the core.
reminders: Feed in spring · prune after fruiting · net fruit.

name: Passionfruit
growing: Full sun on a strong fence, pergola or trellis; north-facing is ideal.
Deep and regular, especially while flowering and fruiting.
Citrus or general fertiliser in spring and summer; too much nitrogen gives leaves, not fruit.
Trim lightly in spring to keep it tidy and productive.
Grafted vines throw suckers from the rootstock; remove them promptly.
Passionvine hopper, fruit fly, fungal diseases in humidity.

cautions.text: Unripe fruit and leaves can upset pets' stomachs.
Eat ripe fruit only; unripe fruit and leaves contain small amounts of cyanogenic compounds.

summary: Vigorous evergreen vine that covers a fence in a season and fruits for 5–7 years.
harvest: Collect fruit when it drops or is fully coloured; it ripens best off the vine for a few days.
reminders: Feed in spring and summer · remove rootstock suckers.

name: Fig
growing: Prune in winter to keep the tree low and picking-height.
Birds, fruit fly, fig rust in humid autumns.
Hardwood cuttings in winter root easily.

cautions.text: Sap and leaves can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs and irritate skin.
Milky sap irritates skin and can cause burns in sunlight; wear gloves when pruning.

summary: Deciduous tree, 3–5 m, with sweet summer fruit. Tolerates poor soil and drought.
harvest: Pick when soft and drooping, from late summer. Figs don't ripen after picking.
reminders: Prune in winter · net fruit in summer.

name: Avocado
growing: Very well-drained; root rot kills avocados in wet soil. Plant on a mound.
Citrus or avocado fertiliser in spring and summer.
Thick coarse mulch, kept off the trunk.
Root rot, fruit spotting bug, possums.
Plant A and B type varieties together for better crops.
Grafted trees; seedlings take many years and fruit poorly.

cautions.text: Leaves, bark and fruit can harm pets, and are highly toxic to birds such as budgies and parrots.

summary: Large evergreen tree, 6–10 m (dwarf types 3–4 m). Needs excellent drainage and takes 3–4 years to fruit.
harvest: Fruit matures on the tree but ripens off it. Pick one and see if it softens in a week.
reminders: Feed spring and summer · mulch thickly · never let it waterlog.

name: Apple
growing: General fruit fertiliser in late winter.
Winter prune to an open vase or espalier.
Fruit fly, codling moth, black spot, birds.
Deciduous; needs some winter chill to fruit.

cautions.text: Seeds, stems and leaves contain cyanogenic compounds; the fruit flesh is fine.
Don't eat large quantities of seeds.

summary: Deciduous fruit tree. On the coast choose low-chill varieties (e.g. Anna, Tropic Sweet) and a pollination partner.
harvest: Pick when fruit twists off easily and seeds are brown.
reminders: Winter prune · feed late winter · fruit fly protection in summer.

name: Peach
growing: Fruit tree fertiliser in late winter.
Prune after fruiting or in winter; peaches fruit on last year's wood.
Fruit fly (net or bag fruit), leaf curl (copper spray at bud swell), brown rot, birds.

tasks.title: Peach: copper spray for leaf curl

cautions.text: Pits, leaves and stems contain cyanogenic compounds; pits are also a choking risk.
Don't eat the kernels.

summary: Deciduous stone fruit tree, 3–4 m. Low-chill varieties fruit on the coast in early summer. Nectarines grow the same way.
harvest: Pick when fruit colours fully and gives slightly near the stem.
reminders: Copper spray at bud swell · net fruit · prune after harvest.

name: Feijoa
growing: Full sun; tolerates wind and salt.
Shape after harvest; hedges can be clipped.
uses: Scoop and eat, smoothies, chutney, crumbles.
Windbreak or hedge with red and white flowers.
summary: Hardy evergreen shrub, 3–4 m, with edible flower petals and aromatic autumn fruit. Makes a good hedge.
harvest: Collect fruit as it drops in autumn; eat within a few days.
reminders: Feed in spring · collect fallen fruit in autumn.

name: Olive
growing: Well-drained, even poor or sandy soil.
Low once established; regular for good fruit.
Prune after harvest to keep the canopy open.
Can self-seed into bushland in some regions; pick up fallen fruit.

cautions.text: Raw olives are inedibly bitter until cured.

summary: Long-lived silver-leaved evergreen, 5–8 m, that loves heat, wind and dry conditions. Fruit must be cured before eating.
harvest: Pick green or black olives in autumn, then brine or cure.
reminders: Prune after harvest · cure fruit in autumn.

name: Grape
growing: Hard winter prune back to 2-bud spurs.
Downy and powdery mildew, birds, fruit fly.
uses: Summer shade, winter sun on a pergola.
Keep dogs away from fallen grapes.

cautions.text: Grapes and raisins are toxic to dogs and can cause kidney failure.

summary: Deciduous climbing vine for pergolas and fences. Choose disease-resistant table varieties for humid coasts.
harvest: Taste-test; pick bunches when sweet, usually late summer.
reminders: Hard prune in winter · net bunches · watch for mildew.

name: Mulberry
growing: Full sun, away from paths and washing lines (purple stains).
Prune after fruiting to control size; dwarf types fruit more after a trim.

cautions.text: Unripe berries can upset pets' stomachs.
Unripe berries and sap can upset stomachs; ripe berries stain.

summary: Fast, tough deciduous tree, 5–10 m (dwarf types 2 m), with heavy spring crops of berries.
harvest: Pick when deep black and soft, September to December.
reminders: Net in spring · prune after fruiting.

name: Banana
growing: Rich, well-drained soil with lots of compost.
Heavy in summer; reduce in winter.
Keep one main stem, one follower and one sucker; remove others.
Cut fruited stems to the ground after harvest.
Grows slowly; leaves can burn in cold.
Suckers. In Queensland and parts of NSW, check local rules before planting.

cautions.text: Sap stains clothing permanently.

summary: Fast tropical plant, 2–5 m. Dwarf types suit warm, frost-free gardens. Each stem fruits once.
harvest: Cut the bunch when fruit is full and the first fingers start to yellow; ripen in the shade.
reminders: Feed monthly in summer · thin suckers.

name: Basil
growing: Full sun, sheltered; morning sun and afternoon shade in heatwaves.
Rich, well-drained soil or potting mix.
Keep evenly moist; water at the base in the morning.
Pinch out tips and flower spikes weekly to keep it bushy and leafy.
Snails on seedlings, downy mildew in humid weather, aphids.
Annual; frost or cold nights below 10°C finish it.
Sow seed or plant seedlings October to January. Tip cuttings root in water.
uses: Pesto, caprese, pasta, pizza, Thai and Italian cooking.
Flowers attract bees; plant near tomatoes.
summary: Fragrant warm-season annual, 40–60 cm. The classic partner for tomatoes; dies with the first cold snap.
harvest: Pick tips from 6 weeks, just above a pair of leaves.
reminders: Plant Oct–Jan · pinch tips weekly · feed every 3 weeks.

name: Thai Basil
growing: Pinch tips regularly; let a few flowers open for bees.
Annual or short-lived perennial in frost-free spots.
Seed or seedlings October to January; cuttings root easily.
summary: Aniseed-flavoured basil with purple stems and flowers. Tougher in heat than sweet basil.
harvest: Pick tips and leaves from 6 weeks.
reminders: Plant Oct–Jan · pinch tips · feed every 3 weeks.

name: Parsley
growing: Pick outer stems; remove flower stalks in its second year, or let it seed.
Few; aphids occasionally. Food plant for swallowtail caterpillars.
Seed is slow (3–4 weeks) — soak overnight. Or plant seedlings year-round.

cautions.text: Can cause skin sensitivity to sunlight in pets that eat large amounts.

summary: Biennial herb grown for leaves. Flat-leaf has more flavour; curly is the classic garnish.
harvest: Pick outer stems from 8 weeks.
reminders: Pick outer stems · feed monthly · resow yearly.

name: Coriander
growing: Full sun in cool months; afternoon shade otherwise.
Sow small batches every 3–4 weeks. Slow-bolt varieties help.
Sow seed direct (it dislikes transplanting); lightly crush seed first.
uses: Thai, Mexican, Indian and Vietnamese dishes; seeds as spice.
summary: Fast annual herb that bolts quickly in heat. Best in autumn, winter and early spring.

glance.sun: Part shade in summer, sun in winter

harvest: Pick leaves from 5–6 weeks. Seeds and green seed pods are also used.
reminders: Sow every 3–4 weeks in cool months.

name: Mint
growing: Keep moist; it wilts fast when dry.
Very invasive in beds. Use a pot, or sink a bottomless bucket into the ground.
Cut back hard after flowering for fresh leaves.
Dies back in cold areas; regrows in spring.
Division or cuttings, which root in water.

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs in large amounts.
Peppermint oil can trigger reflux; pennyroyal (a mint) is toxic and should not be eaten.

summary: Vigorous perennial that spreads by runners. Grow in a pot to keep it contained.
harvest: Pick stems any time.
reminders: Cut back after flowering · feed monthly · keep contained.

name: Chives
growing: Liquid feed monthly in the growing season.
Cut to 5 cm a few times a season for fresh growth. Divide every 2–3 years.
May die back; regrows in spring.
uses: Eggs, potatoes, dips, soups. Flowers in salads.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats, like all onions.

summary: Perennial clump of mild onion-flavoured leaves with edible purple flowers.
harvest: Snip leaves from the base as needed.
reminders: Cut back regularly · divide every few years.

name: Garlic Chives
growing: Cut back to 5 cm for fresh leaves.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats, like all onions.

summary: Flat-leaved perennial with a mild garlic flavour and white flowers. Very hardy.
harvest: Cut leaves as needed.
reminders: Deadhead to stop seeding · cut back for fresh growth.

name: Rosemary
growing: Full sun and good airflow. Handles wind and salt.
Very well-drained, even poor or sandy soil. Hates wet feet.
Water in for the first month, then only in long dry spells.
Trim after flowering; don't cut into bare old wood.
Few; root rot in wet soil.
Tip cuttings in spring or autumn.
uses: Roast lamb and potatoes, bread, oils.
Low hedge; flowers feed bees in winter.
Associated with memory; used in hair rinses.

cautions.text: Avoid large medicinal doses in pregnancy.

summary: Tough, drought-hardy evergreen shrub, 0.5–1.5 m, with blue flowers for bees. Prostrate types trail.
harvest: Snip sprigs any time.
reminders: Trim after flowering · water only when dry.

name: Thyme
growing: Very well-drained, gritty soil; ideal in sandy soil or between pavers.
Trim lightly after flowering to keep it compact; replace every 3–4 years when woody.
Root rot in heavy, wet soil.
uses: Flowers attract bees; good edging plant.
summary: Small woody perennial, 20–30 cm, with tiny aromatic leaves. Lemon thyme is a popular variety.
harvest: Snip sprigs any time.
reminders: Trim after flowering · keep on the dry side.

name: Oregano
growing: Moderate; allow to dry between waterings.
Cut back by half after flowering; cut to ground in late winter.
uses: Pizza, Greek and Italian dishes; dries well.

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten in quantity.

summary: Spreading perennial herb, 30–45 cm, whose flavour is strongest in hot, dry conditions.
harvest: Pick sprigs any time; dry bunches just before flowering for best flavour.
reminders: Cut back after flowering and in late winter.

name: Sage
growing: Allow to dry between waterings; wet humid summers can rot it.
Trim after flowering; replace every 3–4 years.

cautions.text: Avoid large medicinal doses in pregnancy or with epilepsy.

summary: Grey-leaved woody perennial, 50–60 cm. Dislikes humidity, so give it airflow.
harvest: Pick leaves any time.
reminders: Trim after flowering · keep dry.

name: Dill
growing: Sow seed direct in spring and autumn.
summary: Feathery annual, 60–90 cm, grown for leaves and seeds. Runs to seed quickly in heat.
harvest: Pick leaves from 6 weeks; seed heads when brown.
reminders: Sow every 3–4 weeks spring and autumn.

name: Bay Tree
growing: Sun to part shade, sheltered from hot wind.
Clip in spring and summer to shape.
Scale and sooty mould; wipe leaves or spray horticultural oil.

cautions.text: Leaves can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten.
Remove whole leaves before eating; they're a choking hazard. Ornamental "laurels" are different, toxic plants.

summary: Slow-growing evergreen tree that clips well into a hedge or potted topiary.
harvest: Pick leaves any time; dry flat for stronger flavour.
reminders: Clip in spring · check for scale.

name: Vietnamese Mint
growing: Part shade; will grow in boggy spots.
Never let it dry out; a saucer of water under the pot is fine.
Spreads by runners; best in a pot.
Dies back in cold; regrows in spring.
Cuttings root in water within days.
uses: Laksa, Vietnamese salads, rice paper rolls.
summary: Spicy, coriander-like herb that loves warmth and water. Spreads quickly.
harvest: Pick leaves any time.
reminders: Keep wet · feed monthly.

name: Tarragon
growing: Cut back to the ground in late autumn.

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten in quantity.

summary: Perennial with aniseed-flavoured leaves. True French tarragon is grown from cuttings, not seed.
harvest: Pick leaves in spring and summer.
reminders: Cut back in autumn · divide every 3 years.

name: Marjoram

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten in quantity.

summary: Sweeter, milder relative of oregano. Short-lived perennial, 30 cm.
harvest: Pick sprigs any time.
reminders: Trim after flowering.

name: Ginger
growing: Regular in the growing season; much less in winter.
Liquid feed every 3 weeks in summer.
Dies back; keep dry so rhizomes don't rot.
Plant plump supermarket or seed ginger pieces with buds in spring.
summary: Tropical perennial grown from rhizomes. Leafy stems to 1 m die back in winter.
harvest: Young ginger from 4 months; mature rhizomes when leaves die down in late autumn.
reminders: Plant in spring · harvest when leaves die back.

name: Turmeric
growing: Regular in summer; keep drier in winter.
Liquid feed every 3 weeks in summer.

cautions.text: Stains skin and benches orange.

summary: Ginger relative with orange rhizomes and showy flowers. Grows like ginger.
harvest: When leaves yellow and die back, 8–10 months after planting.
reminders: Plant in spring · harvest in late autumn.

name: Curry Leaf
growing: Moderate; dry between waterings in winter.
Citrus or general fertiliser in spring and summer.
Prune to keep bushy; pinch off flowers if you want more leaves.
Suckers and self-seeds in warm areas.
uses: Dhal, curries, chutney; fry leaves in oil to release flavour.

cautions.text: Berries and seeds should not be eaten.
Seeds are toxic; use leaves only.

summary: Small aromatic tree, 2–4 m, whose leaves flavour South Indian cooking. Frost tender.
harvest: Pick leaf stems any time.
reminders: Feed in spring · prune for bushiness.

name: Grevillea
growing: Well-drained, even poor or sandy soil.
Regular for the first year, then only in long dry spells.
Low-phosphorus native fertiliser only, if at all; regular fertilisers can kill them.
Tip prune after flowering to keep it bushy.
Few; root rot in wet soil.
uses: Feeds honeyeaters and bees; good screens and groundcovers.

cautions.text: Generally low risk; some hybrids' foliage can irritate.
Some hybrids (such as 'Robyn Gordon') can cause skin rashes; wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning.

summary: Hardy native shrubs and groundcovers with nectar-rich flowers for much of the year. Sizes from 30 cm to 5 m.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Tip prune after flowering · native fertiliser only.

name: Bottlebrush
growing: Full sun; handles wind and wet spots.
Most soils, including heavy and damp ones.
Cut off spent flowers just behind the brush for more blooms and a denser shape.
uses: Nectar for birds and bees; hedges and screens.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Tough native shrubs, 1–4 m, with red, pink or white brush flowers in spring and autumn.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Prune after flowering · native feed in spring.

name: Kangaroo Paw
growing: Very well-drained, sandy soil; ideal for the peninsula.
Cut flower stems to the base after flowering; cut old leaves back in late winter.
Ink disease (black leaves) in humid conditions; remove affected leaves.

tasks.title: Kangaroo paw: cut back old leaves
Kangaroo paw: remove spent flower stems

cautions.text: Non-toxic.
Fine hairs can irritate sensitive skin.

summary: Strappy native perennial with velvety paw-shaped flowers in spring and summer. Dwarf types suit pots.
harvest: Cut flowers last well in vases.
reminders: Cut back after flowering and in late winter.

name: Lilly Pilly
growing: Clip in spring and summer for a dense hedge.
Psyllids cause pimply leaves; choose resistant varieties such as 'Resilience'.
summary: Dense native rainforest shrubs and trees with colourful new growth and edible berries. Popular hedges.
harvest: Pick ripe berries in autumn and winter.
reminders: Clip spring and summer · feed in spring.

name: Westringia
growing: Full sun; handles salt spray and wind.
Clip a few times a year for a hedge or ball shape.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Grey-green native shrub, 1–2 m, with small white or mauve flowers. One of the toughest coastal plants.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Clip a few times a year.

name: Lomandra
growing: Cut back hard every few years in late winter to refresh.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.
Leaves have sharp edges.

summary: Tough native grass-like clump, 60 cm–1 m. Handles sun, shade, drought and wet.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Cut back every few years in late winter.

name: Banksia
growing: Light tip prune; avoid cutting into old wood.
uses: Nectar for birds and possums; coastal gardens.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Iconic native shrubs and trees with candle flower spikes. Coast banksia handles sand and salt.
harvest: Old cones are decorative.
reminders: Native feed sparingly in spring.

name: Correa
uses: Winter nectar for honeyeaters; shade gardens.

cautions.text: Non-toxic.

summary: Compact native shrub, 0.5–1.5 m, with bell flowers through autumn and winter when little else flowers.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Trim after flowering in spring.

name: Finger Lime
growing: Citrus fertiliser in spring and late summer.
Citrus pests such as scale and leaf miner.

cautions.text: Leaves and peel can upset pets' stomachs.
Very sharp thorns; wear gloves.

summary: Thorny native citrus shrub, 2–4 m, with finger-shaped fruit full of juicy pearls.
harvest: Pick when fruit comes away easily, usually summer to autumn.
reminders: Citrus feed spring and late summer.

name: Warrigal Greens
uses: Blanched, then used like spinach in pies, pasta and stir-fries.

cautions.text: High oxalate leaves can upset pets in quantity.
Blanch leaves in boiling water for a minute and discard the water before eating, to remove oxalates.

summary: Sprawling native leafy green that thrives in heat, sand and salt where English spinach bolts.
harvest: Pick tips and young leaves any time.
reminders: Pick tips often · blanch before eating.

name: Monstera
growing: Bright, indirect light; no harsh afternoon sun through glass.
When the top 5 cm is dry; less in winter.
Liquid indoor plant food monthly in spring and summer.
Moss pole for climbing and bigger leaves.
Wipe dust off leaves. Repot every 2 years.
Stem cuttings with a node and aerial root.
uses: Keep away from pets and children.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats; causes mouth pain and drooling if chewed.
Sap irritates skin and mouth. Unripe fruit is irritant.

summary: Big-leaved climbing aroid. Grows indoors in bright light or outdoors in shade on the coast.
harvest: Fruit on mature outdoor plants is edible only when fully ripe.
reminders: Water when top 5 cm dry · feed monthly in warm months.

name: Peace Lily
growing: Low to bright indirect light; flowers better in brighter spots.
Keep slightly moist; water as soon as it starts to droop.
Half-strength liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Wipe leaves; brown tips mean dry air or tap-water salts.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats; causes mouth irritation and drooling. (Not a true lily.)
Sap irritates skin and mouth.

summary: Easy indoor plant with white flowers that tolerates low light. Droops dramatically when thirsty.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when droopy · feed monthly in warm months.

name: Pothos
growing: When the top half of the mix is dry.
Liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Trim long vines to keep it bushy; cuttings root in water.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats if chewed.
Sap irritates skin and mouth.

summary: Trailing or climbing indoor vine that tolerates low light and neglect.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when half dry · trim long vines.

name: Snake Plant
growing: Any light from low to bright.
Only when completely dry; every 3–4 weeks, less in winter. Overwatering is the main killer.

tasks.title: Snake plant: check soil and water

cautions.text: Can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if chewed.

summary: Upright, nearly indestructible indoor plant that tolerates low light and drought.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water only when dry.

name: ZZ Plant
growing: Light feed in spring and summer.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats if chewed.
Sap irritates skin; wash hands after handling.

summary: Glossy, drought-tolerant indoor plant that copes with low light.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when fully dry.

name: Fiddle Leaf Fig
growing: Very bright, indirect light near a window; keep away from draughts and air conditioning.
When the top 5 cm is dry; less in winter.
Liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Wipe leaves; rotate a quarter turn monthly for even growth. Leaf drop usually means it was moved or overwatered.

tasks.title: Fiddle leaf fig: feed and rotate

cautions.text: Sap can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs and irritate skin.
Milky sap irritates skin.

summary: Indoor tree with big violin-shaped leaves. Likes bright light and hates being moved.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when top 5 cm dry · rotate monthly.

name: Spider Plant
growing: When the top few cm are dry.
Liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Brown tips usually mean fluoride in tap water or dry air.
uses: Hanging baskets; a safe choice for homes with pets.

cautions.text: Non-toxic to dogs and cats (cats may chew it).

summary: Easy, pet-friendly indoor plant with arching striped leaves and dangling baby plants.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when top dry · pot up babies.

name: Rubber Plant
growing: When the top 5 cm is dry.
Liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Prune the top to make it branch; wear gloves.

cautions.text: Sap can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs.
Milky sap irritates skin.

summary: Glossy-leaved indoor tree that's more forgiving than the fiddle leaf fig.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when top 5 cm dry · feed monthly in warm months.

name: Heartleaf Philodendron
growing: When the top few cm are dry.
Liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Pinch long stems to keep it full.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats if chewed.
Sap irritates skin and mouth.

summary: Fast trailing vine with heart-shaped leaves; one of the easiest indoor plants.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when top dry · pinch long stems.

name: Aloe Vera
growing: Outdoors in full sun to part shade.
uses: Gel soothes minor burns and sunburn.
Don't eat it; keep away from pets.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats if eaten; causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
The yellow latex under the skin is a strong laxative; use only the clear gel on skin.

summary: Succulent with fleshy leaves whose gel soothes minor burns. Grows indoors or outdoors in sun.
harvest: Cut an outer leaf and use the clear gel.
reminders: Water only when dry.

name: Boston Fern
growing: Bright, indirect light with humidity; bathrooms are ideal.
Keep evenly moist; mist in dry weather.
Half-strength liquid feed monthly in warm months.
Brown fronds mean dry air or dry soil; trim them off.

cautions.text: Non-toxic to dogs and cats.

summary: Lush, pet-safe fern for humid bathrooms, verandahs and hanging baskets.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Keep moist · mist in dry weather.

name: Moth Orchid
growing: Bright, indirect light; east window is ideal.
When roots turn silvery, usually weekly; drain well. Never leave water in the crown.
Orchid fertiliser at quarter strength every 2 weeks.
After flowering, cut the spike above the second node for a second flush, or at the base to rest the plant.

cautions.text: Non-toxic to dogs and cats.

summary: Easy indoor orchid whose flower sprays last for months.
harvest: Not harvested.
reminders: Water when roots silver · weak feed fortnightly.

name: Tomato
growing: 6–8 hours of sun, sheltered from strong wind. Don't plant where tomatoes, potatoes or eggplant grew in the last 3 years.
Rich, well-drained, pH 6–7. Dig in compost and aged manure; add a handful of dolomite lime to acidic soils.
Deeply 2–3 times a week at the base. Irregular watering causes blossom-end rot and split fruit. Mulch well.
Liquid tomato food every 2 weeks once flowers appear. Too much nitrogen gives leaves, not fruit.
Stake or cage tall types at planting; tie in loosely every 30 cm as they grow.
Pinch out side shoots (laterals) below the first flower truss on tall types. Leave bush types unpruned.
Queensland fruit fly, tomato grub, whitefly and leaf spot. Net or bag fruit from December; remove spotted lower leaves.
Grows as an annual. In frost-free spots a late crop can carry into early winter.
Sow seed indoors in late winter, or plant seedlings from late September once nights stay above 10°C.
uses: Salads, sauces, roasting, passata and chutney.
Plant basil and marigolds nearby to attract pollinators and predatory insects.

tasks.title: Tomato: plant out seedlings
tasks.notes: Plant deep, up to the first leaves; stake now.

tasks.title: Tomato: liquid feed
tasks.notes: Tomato food around the base once flowering.

tasks.title: Tomato: fruit fly protection
tasks.notes: Bag or net fruit, set traps, pick up fallen fruit.

tasks.title: Tomato: tie in and remove laterals
tasks.notes: Tie stems to stakes; pinch side shoots on tall types.

cautions.text: Leaves, stems and green fruit can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten. Ripe fruit is fine.
Leaves and stems are not edible. Sap can irritate sensitive skin; wear gloves when pruning.

summary: Warm-season fruiting vegetable. Tall (indeterminate) types climb 1.5–2 m; bush types stay under 1 m. Crops summer to autumn.
harvest: From 10–12 weeks. Pick when fully coloured and slightly soft, or pick at first blush and ripen indoors to beat fruit fly.
reminders: Plant out Oct · feed fortnightly Nov–Feb · net against fruit fly from Dec · tie in weekly.

name: Cherry Tomato
growing: Full sun with shelter from wind. Great in large pots and hanging baskets (trailing types).
Rich, well-drained potting mix or garden soil with compost.
Keep evenly moist; pots may need daily water in summer.
Liquid tomato food every 2 weeks from flowering.
Stake or trellis; vines sprawl without support.
Light pruning only; remove crowded or yellowing lower leaves for airflow.
Less troubled by fruit fly than big tomatoes, but net in bad years. Watch for whitefly.
Annual. Often self-seeds and pops up next spring.
Seedlings from September to December; seed indoors in late winter.
uses: Snacking, salads, roasting whole, quick sauces.
Productive in small spaces; children love picking them.

cautions.text: Leaves, stems and green fruit can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten. Ripe fruit is fine.
Leaves and stems are not edible. Small round fruit is a choking risk for toddlers; cut in half.

summary: Small-fruited tomato that crops heavily and handles heat and humidity better than large types. Vigorous vines to 2 m.

glance.indoors: Possible on a very sunny balcony

harvest: From 8–10 weeks, every few days through summer. Pick whole trusses when most fruit is coloured.
reminders: Plant out Oct–Nov · feed fortnightly Nov–Mar · pick every few days.

name: Capsicum
growing: Full sun, warm and sheltered. Needs warmth to set fruit.
Even moisture; drying out causes flower drop. Mulch.
Potassium-rich liquid feed every 2 weeks from flowering.
Stake once fruit forms; branches are brittle.
Fruit fly, aphids, sunburn on fruit in heatwaves (keep leaf cover).
Grown as an annual; may survive a mild winter if pruned back.
Seedlings in October–November once the soil is warm.
uses: Raw in salads, roasted, stuffed, stir-fries.
Pairs well with basil and marigolds.

tasks.title: Capsicum: feed and check fruit fly

summary: Sweet, mild-fruited relative of chilli. Bushy plants 60–90 cm that crop from midsummer into autumn.
harvest: Pick green from about 10 weeks, or leave to colour red, yellow or orange for sweeter fruit. Cut with secateurs.
reminders: Plant Oct–Nov · feed fortnightly from flowering · net fruit from Dec.

name: Eggplant
growing: Rich, well-drained, with plenty of compost.
Deep, regular watering; mulch to keep roots cool and moist.
Liquid feed every 2 weeks once flowering.
Stake when fruit begins to swell.
Twenty-eight spotted ladybird, whitefly, spider mites in dry heat.
Annual; finishes when nights cool in autumn.
Seedlings from late October into warm soil.
uses: Grilled, baba ganoush, curries, moussaka, stir-fries.

cautions.text: Leaves and stems can upset dogs' and cats' stomachs if eaten.
Leaves are not edible. Some varieties have small spines on the calyx.

summary: Heat-loving fruiting vegetable, 60–100 cm tall, with glossy purple, white or striped fruit from midsummer.
harvest: When skin is glossy and springs back when pressed, from about 12 weeks. Dull skin means overripe and seedy.
reminders: Plant late Oct · feed fortnightly · pick while glossy.

name: Zucchini
growing: Full sun with room to spread.
Rich soil with compost; plant on a slight mound for drainage.
Deeply at the base, keeping leaves dry to reduce powdery mildew.
Liquid feed every 2 weeks once flowering.
If fruit shrivels, hand-pollinate: brush a male flower onto female flowers (those with a tiny fruit behind).
Powdery mildew (late summer), pumpkin beetle, fruit rot in wet weather.
Annual; pull out once mildew takes over in autumn.
Sow seed direct or plant seedlings from October to January.
uses: Grilled, fritters, bread, soups. Flowers can be stuffed and fried.

tasks.title: Zucchini: sow or plant
tasks.notes: A second sowing in January extends the harvest.

tasks.title: Zucchini: pick and check
tasks.notes: Pick small fruit; hand-pollinate if fruit shrivels.

cautions.text: Very bitter fruit can contain cucurbitacins and cause stomach upset; don't eat bitter-tasting zucchini.

summary: Fast, productive bushy squash about 1 m wide. Crops within 8 weeks of planting through summer.
harvest: Pick at 15–20 cm, every 2–3 days in peak season. Missed fruit quickly becomes marrows.
reminders: Plant Oct–Jan · pick every 2–3 days · watch for mildew from Feb.

name: Cucumber
growing: Even moisture; dry spells make fruit bitter.
Liquid feed every 2 weeks once flowering.
Grow up a 1.5 m trellis to save space and keep fruit clean.
Sow direct or plant from October to January.
uses: Trellised vines make a summer screen.

tasks.title: Cucumber: plant and set up trellis

cautions.text: Bitter fruit can cause stomach upset; discard it.

summary: Climbing or sprawling warm-season vine. Lebanese and apple types suit home gardens and crop through summer.
harvest: Pick young and firm, from about 8 weeks, every few days.
reminders: Plant Oct–Jan · train up trellis · pick every few days.

name: Pumpkin
growing: Full sun with lots of room; can sprawl over a compost heap or fence.
Rich soil; plant into a mound of compost.
Deeply once or twice a week, at the base.
Liquid feed every 2–3 weeks until fruit sets.
Hand-pollinate early in the morning if fruit doesn't set. Put a tile under ripening fruit to prevent rot.
Powdery mildew, pumpkin beetle, fruit fly stings on young fruit.
uses: Roasting, soup, scones, curries. Cured pumpkins store for months.

tasks.title: Pumpkin: sow seed
tasks.notes: Sow 2–3 seeds per mound; thin to the strongest.

tasks.title: Pumpkin: check for ripeness
tasks.notes: Harvest when stalks are dry and corky; cure in sun.

summary: Rambling vine that spreads 3–5 m and ripens storable pumpkins by autumn. Butternut and Jap types are reliable.
harvest: When vines die back and stalks dry and crack (about 16 weeks). Cut with 5 cm of stalk; cure in the sun for 2 weeks.
reminders: Sow Oct–Dec · feed until fruit sets · harvest when stalks dry.

name: Lettuce
growing: Full sun in winter, afternoon shade in summer to stop bolting.
Little and often; never let it dry out.
Liquid feed every 2 weeks for tender growth.
Sow small batches every 3–4 weeks for a continuous supply. Summer heat makes it bolt and turn bitter.
Sow seed or plant seedlings year-round; choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer.

tasks.title: Lettuce: sow next batch
tasks.notes: Sow a short row every 3–4 weeks.

summary: Quick leafy salad crop. Loose-leaf types can be picked leaf by leaf for weeks. Grows year-round on the coast.
harvest: Pick outer leaves of loose-leaf types from 4–6 weeks, or cut whole heads at 8–10 weeks.
reminders: Sow every 3–4 weeks · liquid feed fortnightly · snail checks.

name: English Spinach
growing: Full sun in winter; part shade in warmer months.
Rich, well-drained soil with compost; pH 6.5–7.
Bolts in hot, long days; for summer greens grow silverbeet or Warrigal greens instead.
Sow seed direct March to August.

cautions.text: High oxalate leaves can upset pets in quantity.
High in oxalates; people prone to kidney stones may want to limit large amounts.

summary: Cool-season leafy green that bolts quickly in heat. Best sown autumn to early spring.
harvest: Pick outer leaves from 6 weeks.
reminders: Sow Mar–Aug · feed fortnightly.

name: Silverbeet
growing: Sun to part shade; tolerates heat better than spinach.
Regular; mulch to keep soil moist.
Liquid feed every 2–3 weeks to keep leaves coming.
Pick outer stems regularly; remove flower stalks.
Snails, leaf spot in humid weather (remove spotted leaves).

cautions.text: Oxalates can upset pets in quantity.
Contains oxalates; cooking reduces them.

summary: Tough, productive leafy green that crops for a year or more. Coloured-stem types are ornamental.
harvest: Twist off outer stems from 8 weeks; leave the centre to keep growing.
reminders: Pick outer leaves weekly · feed every 3 weeks.

name: Kale
growing: Full sun; part shade in summer.
Rich, slightly alkaline soil with compost; add lime to acidic soil.
Cabbage white caterpillars and aphids. Net plants in warm months.
Plant seedlings February to May for the best crop.

cautions.text: Large amounts can upset pets' stomachs.

summary: Hardy leafy brassica, 60–90 cm, that crops through autumn, winter and spring.
harvest: Pick lower leaves from 8 weeks, leaving the top to keep growing.
reminders: Plant Feb–May · net against caterpillars · pick lower leaves.

name: Broccoli
growing: Rich, slightly alkaline soil with compost; lime acidic soils.
Nitrogen-rich liquid feed every 2 weeks until heads form.
Cabbage white caterpillars and aphids; net seedlings.

cautions.text: Large amounts can upset pets' stomachs.

summary: Cool-season brassica that forms a central head, then side shoots for weeks after.
harvest: Cut the central head while buds are tight (10–14 weeks), then pick side shoots.
reminders: Plant Feb–May · net · cut heads while tight.

name: Cabbage
growing: Rich, slightly alkaline soil with compost.
Cabbage white caterpillars, aphids, slugs; net plants.

cautions.text: Large amounts can upset pets' stomachs.

summary: Cool-season brassica forming a dense head. Mini and savoy types suit small gardens.
harvest: Cut when heads are firm, 10–16 weeks depending on type.
reminders: Plant Feb–Jun · net · cut when firm.

name: Cauliflower
growing: Rich, slightly alkaline soil with compost and a little lime.
Keep evenly moist; stress causes small, early heads.
When the curd appears, fold leaves over it to keep it white.

cautions.text: Large amounts can upset pets' stomachs.

summary: Cool-season brassica forming a white or coloured curd. Needs steady growth to head well.
harvest: Cut when the curd is firm and tight, 14–20 weeks.
reminders: Plant Feb–Apr · cover curds · cut when tight.

name: Carrot
growing: Loose, deep and stone-free; sandy peninsula soil is ideal. No fresh manure (causes forked roots).
Keep the surface moist until seedlings appear (2–3 weeks), then water deeply weekly.
Low-nitrogen; a little potash once up is enough.
Thin seedlings to 5 cm apart. Cover shoulders with soil to stop greening.
Carrot fly is rare in Australia; aphids occasionally.
Sow seed direct, mixed with sand for even spacing.
summary: Root crop sown direct. Short varieties suit pots and heavy soil. Grows most of the year on the coast.
harvest: From 10–14 weeks, when shoulders are about 2 cm across.
reminders: Sow every 4–6 weeks · thin seedlings · keep moist until up.

name: Beetroot
growing: Well-drained soil with compost; add a little lime to acidic soils.
Each seed is a cluster; thin seedlings to 10 cm apart.
Soak seed overnight, then sow direct August to April.

cautions.text: Oxalate-rich leaves can upset pets in quantity.
Can turn urine pink, which is harmless.

summary: Easy root crop with edible leaves. Sown direct most of the year.
harvest: From 8–10 weeks, when roots are golf-ball to tennis-ball size. Young leaves are good in salads.
reminders: Sow Aug–Apr · thin seedlings · pick young.

name: Radish
growing: Full sun; part shade in summer.
Keep moist; dry soil makes radishes hot and woody.
Sow small amounts every 2 weeks; good for marking rows of slow seeds.
uses: Salads, pickles, roasted. Young leaves are edible.
summary: The fastest root crop, ready in 4–6 weeks. Daikon types grow large over winter.
harvest: Pull when 2–3 cm across, 4–6 weeks after sowing.
reminders: Sow every 2 weeks · pull young.

name: Potato
growing: Full sun. Rotate; don't follow tomatoes or eggplant.
Loose, slightly acidic soil with compost.
Regular once shoots appear, especially while flowering.
Hill soil or mulch around stems as they grow so tubers stay covered and don't turn green.
Potato moth, leaf blights in humid weather.
Plant certified seed potatoes 10 cm deep, August–September and again in February.
uses: Store in the dark; discard green potatoes.

tasks.title: Potato: hill up
tasks.notes: Mound soil or straw around stems.

cautions.text: Leaves, stems, green and raw potatoes are toxic to dogs and cats.
Green or sprouting potatoes contain solanine; don't eat green parts. Leaves and berries are toxic.

summary: Tuber crop planted from seed potatoes. Grows well in beds, bags or tyre stacks.
harvest: New potatoes when plants flower; main crop when foliage dies down, 14–18 weeks.
reminders: Plant Aug–Sep and Feb · hill up every few weeks · harvest when foliage dies.

name: Sweet Potato
growing: Full sun, the warmest spot available.
Light, sandy, well-drained soil; too much nitrogen gives leaves, not tubers.
Lift vines occasionally so they don't root along the ground.
Sweet potato weevil in the north; few pests on the coast.
Plant rooted slips October to December.
uses: Roasted, mashed, chips. Young leaves can be cooked like spinach.
summary: Sprawling tropical vine grown from slips. Loves heat and sandy soil; crops in autumn.
harvest: After 4–5 months when leaves yellow, before cold weather. Dig carefully; skins bruise easily.
reminders: Plant slips Oct–Dec · dig in autumn.

name: Onion
growing: Well-drained soil with compost; add lime to acidic soil.
Regular while bulbing; stop once tops start to fall.
Light, balanced feed; excess nitrogen gives soft bulbs.
Thrips, downy mildew in wet springs.
Sow seed or plant seedlings April to June.
uses: Keep onion scraps away from pets.

tasks.title: Onion: check for harvest
tasks.notes: Lift when tops fall over; cure in sun.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats in all forms (raw, cooked, powder). Can cause anaemia.

summary: Bulb crop sown in autumn and harvested in late spring and summer. Choose varieties suited to your latitude.
harvest: When tops yellow and fall over (6–8 months). Dry in the sun for a week before storing.
reminders: Plant Apr–Jun · weed regularly · lift when tops fall.

name: Garlic
growing: Regular through winter and spring; stop a few weeks before harvest.
Light balanced feed in late winter.
Remove flower stalks (scapes) on hardneck types; they're edible.
Rust in humid springs; few others.
Plant cloves pointy end up, 5 cm deep, March to May. Use Australian-grown seed garlic.
uses: Everything savoury. Scapes and green garlic are good in stir-fries.
Used for colds and general health.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats in all forms.
Can irritate skin of sensitive people when handled in quantity.

summary: Planted from cloves in autumn and harvested in early summer. Easy and rewarding.
harvest: When the lower third of leaves yellow, usually November–December. Dry bunches in the shade.
reminders: Plant Mar–May · harvest Nov–Dec.

name: Spring Onion
growing: Cut stems 3 cm above the base and they regrow. Divide clumps every year.
Seed year-round, or replant the root ends from shop-bought bunches.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats.

summary: Perennial onion grown for its green stems. Grows year-round and regrows after cutting.
harvest: From 8 weeks; cut as needed.
reminders: Cut as needed · feed monthly.

name: Leek
growing: Plant seedlings in deep holes and hill soil around stems to blanch them white.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs and cats.

summary: Mild onion relative with long white stems, grown through autumn and winter.
harvest: From 4–5 months when stems are 2–3 cm thick.
reminders: Plant Feb–May · hill up · feed every 3 weeks.

name: Peas
growing: Well-drained soil; add lime to acidic soil. Don't over-fertilise.
Little needed; peas fix their own nitrogen.
A 1.5 m trellis or netting for climbing types.
Powdery mildew late in the season; birds on seedlings.
Sow seed direct March to July. Don't soak; seed rots in cold, wet soil.
uses: Leaves nitrogen in the soil for the next crop; dig spent plants in.

tasks.title: Peas: sow seed and set up trellis

summary: Cool-season climbing legume. Sugar snaps are eaten pod and all.
harvest: Pick often from 10–12 weeks while pods are plump and sweet.
reminders: Sow Mar–Jul · trellis · pick often.

name: Snow Peas
growing: Well-drained soil with a little lime.
Sow seed direct March to July.
summary: Flat-podded pea eaten whole. Climbing types crop for weeks through winter and spring.
harvest: Pick flat pods before seeds swell, every couple of days.
reminders: Sow Mar–Jul · pick every 2 days.

name: Bush Beans
growing: Well-drained soil; no extra nitrogen needed.
Sow every 4 weeks for a steady supply.
Bean fly, two-spotted mite, rust in humidity.
Sow seed direct September to February into warm soil.

cautions.text: Raw beans can upset pets' stomachs; cooked plain beans are fine.
Don't eat dry beans raw; they must be boiled.

summary: Compact warm-season bean, 40–60 cm, that crops quickly with no support.
harvest: Pick young pods from 8–10 weeks, every few days.
reminders: Sow every 4 weeks Sep–Feb · pick every few days.

name: Climbing Beans
growing: Full sun against a fence or teepee.
Strong trellis, strings or teepee 2 m+.
Sow seed direct September to January.

cautions.text: Raw beans can upset pets' stomachs.
Don't eat dry beans raw; they must be boiled.

summary: Vigorous climbers to 2–3 m that crop for months. Scarlet runners have showy red flowers.
harvest: Pick young pods often from 10–12 weeks; picking keeps them producing.
reminders: Sow Sep–Jan · pick often.

name: Sweet Corn
growing: Full sun. Plant in a block of at least 4 × 4, not a single row, for pollination.
Rich soil with compost and manure.
Deep, regular watering, especially when tassels appear.
Sow seed direct October to January.

tasks.title: Sweet corn: sow in a block
Sweet corn: check cobs
tasks.notes: Ripe when silks brown and kernels are milky.

cautions.text: Cobs are a choking and bowel-blockage risk for dogs; keep cobs away.

summary: Tall warm-season grass, 1.5–2 m, grown in blocks for wind pollination.
harvest: About 3 weeks after silks appear, when silks brown and kernels squirt milky juice.
reminders: Sow in blocks Oct–Jan · feed every 3 weeks · check silks.

name: Asparagus
growing: Full sun in a permanent bed.
Deep, well-drained soil with lots of compost.
Don't harvest the first year and only lightly the second. Let ferns grow after harvest season.
Cut yellow ferns to the ground in late autumn and mulch.

cautions.text: Red berries on female plants can upset pets' stomachs.
Berries are not edible.

summary: Long-lived perennial that sends up spears each spring for 15+ years once established.
harvest: Snap spears at 15–20 cm from September to November in year three onwards.
reminders: Plant crowns in winter · cut ferns in late autumn · harvest spring.

name: Rhubarb
growing: Sun, with afternoon shade in hot areas.
Rich, well-drained soil with plenty of manure.
Regular; doesn't like to dry out.
Manure or compost in spring and autumn.
Remove flower stalks so energy goes to leaves.
Plant crowns in winter; divide every 4–5 years.

tasks.title: Rhubarb: feed
tasks.notes: Manure or compost around the crown.

cautions.text: Leaves are toxic to dogs, cats and livestock (oxalates).
Leaves are poisonous; eat only the stalks.

summary: Perennial with tart red stalks used like fruit. Crops for years from one crown.
harvest: Pull (don't cut) stalks from the base once established, leaving at least a third of the plant.
reminders: Feed spring and autumn · remove flowers · pull stalks.

name: Celery
growing: Never let it dry out; stringy, bitter stalks mean thirst.

cautions.text: Handling in sunlight can cause skin sensitivity in rare cases.

summary: Slow, thirsty crop that needs constant moisture. Self-blanching types are easiest.
harvest: From 14–16 weeks; pick outer stalks or cut the whole plant.
reminders: Water often · feed fortnightly.

name: Bok Choy
growing: Sun in winter, part shade in summer.
Sow seed or plant seedlings February to October.
uses: Stir-fries, soups, steamed with oyster sauce.
summary: Fast Asian green ready in 6–8 weeks. Best in the cooler months.
harvest: Cut whole heads at 6–8 weeks or pick outer leaves.
reminders: Sow every few weeks Feb–Oct.

name: Rocket
growing: Sun in winter, part shade in summer.
Pick often; flowers are edible but leaves get hotter once it bolts.
summary: Peppery salad green that grows fast and self-seeds. Wild rocket is a longer-lived perennial.
harvest: Pick leaves from 4 weeks.
reminders: Sow every 4 weeks · pick often.
